newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian government tries to end budget stand-off.
newsitem.headline: Italian government tries to end budget stand-off.

text.p: The Italian government urged the opposition on Tuesday to return to parliament to discuss the 1997 budget after the centre-right bloc walked out of the lower house in protest at the austerity package.
Silvio Berlusconi's centre-right Freedom Alliance and the separatist Northern League announced on Monday that they would no longer attend parliamentary debate on the budget.
Their move challenges the legitimacy of any vote on a budget Prime Minister Romano Prodi says is vital to Italy's hopes of becoming a founder member of the Europe Union's planned single currency.
The boycott was mounted in protest at a government request to set policy in several key areas -- especially on fiscal reform -- without recourse to parliamentary approval.
Seeking to end the opposition revolt, Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco gave more details of the planned revision of income tax in a speech to parliament on Tuesday.
"I hope that this proposal will be enough to reassure people," Visco said.
The opposition gave the speech a cool reception but said it would meet later to discuss the situation.

The 1997 budget, which aims to slice 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) off next year's deficit to enable Italy join the single currency, has proved hugely unpopular and helped galvanise Berlusconi's previously divided opposition alliance.

More than half a million people marched through Rome at the weekend to protest against tax rises in the budget, sending a shiver through the government and spurring the opposition to announce their parliamentary walkout.

The boycott has also generated strains within Prodi's six-month-old coalition, an alliance that groups centrists and leftists and depends for survival on external support from the hardline Communist Refoundation Party.
"If it were not for the fact that the budget is at stake, the Prodi government could have run the risk of falling," the newspaper La Stampa said.
The walk-out has handed more power to Communist Refoundation. Without the opposition, Refoundation now ensures the legal quorum in the lower house of parliament and can halt debate at any moment.

The party is opposed to any attempt by Prodi to seek a compromise with Berlusconi. In a show of power, it briefly withdrew from parliament on Monday night on word that behind-the-scenes talks were going on.
The muscle-flexing drew howls of protest from coalition parties, anxious about hard-left influence over government and the damage this might do to their own electoral standing.
"Don't they realise this is political suicide," said Lanfranco Turci, a senior member of the largest coalition partner, the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS).
"They have an atomic bomb and insist on always using it."

An opinion poll published on Tuesday showed that the Freedom Alliance was once again the most popular political grouping in Italy, drawing support from 46.2 percent of the electorate against 42.1 percent at the last general election in April.
By contrast the main coalition parties won just 33.2 percent against 34.7 percent in April, while support for Communist Refoundation rose to 10.9 percent from 8.6 percent.
The survey, by Datamedia, questioned 1,503 people on Monday.
